user_input: If I don't configure anything, how long can a single test run before Playwright kills it, and what counts toward that budget?
reference: Each test gets 30 seconds out of the box, and that budget covers the test body plus fixture setup and any beforeEach hooks.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
llm_response:
If you do not configure anything, a single test can run for 30 seconds before Playwright kills it.

The time counted toward this 30-second budget includes:
*   The test function itself.
*   Fixture setups.
*   `beforeEach` hooks.
llm_references:
Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

Timed out test produces the following error:

```
`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.`
```

Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

user_input: How long does a web-first assertion like toHaveText keep retrying before giving up, if I leave the defaults?
reference: Web-first assertions retry for about 5 seconds by default, and that clock runs independently of the overall test timeout.
reference_contexts: Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text) have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout. It produces the following error:
llm_response: If you leave the defaults, a web-first assertion like `toHaveText` will retry for 5 seconds before giving up [1, 2].
llm_references:
Playwright includes test assertions in the form of
`expect`
function. To make an assertion, call
`expect(value)`
and choose a matcher that reflects the expectation. There are many
generic matchers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-genericassertions)
like
`toEqual`
,
`toContain`
,
`toBeTruthy`
that can be used to assert any conditions.

```
`expect(success).toBeTruthy();`
```

Playwright also includes web-specific
async matchers (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions)
that will wait until the expected condition is met. Consider the following example:

```
`awaitexpect(page.getByTestId('status')).toHaveText('Submitted');`
```

Playwright will be re-testing the element with the test id of
`status`
until the fetched element has the
`"Submitted"`
text. It will re-fetch the element and check it over and over, until the condition is met or until the timeout is reached. You can either pass this timeout or configure it once via the
testConfig.expect (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testconfig#test-config-expect)
value in the test config.

By default, the timeout for assertions is set to 5 seconds. Learn more about
various timeouts (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-timeouts)
.

Auto-retrying assertions like
expect(locator).toHaveText() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locatorassertions#locator-assertions-to-have-text)
have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout. It produces the following error:

```
`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Error: expect(received).toHaveText(expected)Expected string: "my text"Received string: ""Call log:- expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms- waiting for "locator('button')"`
```

example.spec.ts
```
`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('example',async({page})=>{awaitexpect(locator).toHaveText('hello',{timeout:10_000});});`
```

user_input: I have a flaky test I'd like re-run a couple of times on failure — what's the quickest command-line way?
reference: Pass a retry count on the run command, e.g. npx playwright test --retries=3 re-runs failing tests up to three times. Nothing is retried unless you opt in.
reference_contexts: Playwright supports test retries . When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.
llm_response:
The quickest command-line way to re-run failing tests is to use the `--retries` flag with `npx playwright test`.

For example, to give failing tests 3 retry attempts, use:
`npx playwright test --retries=3`
llm_references:
Playwright supports
test retries
. When enabled, failing tests will be retried multiple times until they pass, or until the maximum number of retries is reached. By default failing tests are not retried.

```
`# Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsnpx playwrighttest--retries=3`
```

You can configure retries in the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts
```
`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({// Give failing tests 3 retry attemptsretries:3,});`
```

Playwright Test will categorize tests as follows:

"passed" - tests that passed on the first run;
"flaky" - tests that failed on the first run, but passed when retried;
"failed" - tests that failed on the first run and failed all retries.

```
`Running3tests using1worker✓ example.spec.ts:4:2 › first passes(438ms)x example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(691ms)✓ example.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky(522ms)✓ example.spec.ts:6:2 › third passes(932ms)1flakyexample.spec.ts:5:2 › second flaky2passed(4s)`
```

You can detect retries at runtime with
testInfo.retry (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-retry)
, which is accessible to any test, hook or fixture. Here is an example that clears some server-side state before a retry.

```
`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('my test',async({page},testInfo)=>{if(testInfo.retry)awaitcleanSomeCachesOnTheServer();// ...});`
```

You can specify retries for a specific group of tests or a single file with
test.describe.configure() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-describe-configure)
.

```
`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test.describe(()=>{// All tests in this describe group will get 2 retry attempts.test.describe.configure({retries:2});test('test 1',async({page})=>{// ...});test('test 2',async({page})=>{// ...});});`
```

user_input: Do I get videos of my test runs automatically, or do I have to switch them on?
reference: They stay off unless you opt in; a single config setting — video — turns recording on and selects the mode.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test can record videos for your tests, controlled by the video option in your Playwright config. By default videos are off.
llm_response:
You have to switch them on. By default, videos are off. You can control video recording using the `video` option in your Playwright config.

The available settings are:
*   `'off'`: Do not record video.
*   `'on'`: Record video for each test.
*   `'retain-on-failure'`: Record video for each test, but remove all videos from successful test runs.
*   `'on-first-retry'`: Record video only when retrying a test for the first time.
llm_references:
Playwright Test can record videos for your tests, controlled by the
`video`
option in your Playwright config. By default videos are off.

`'off'`
- Do not record video.
`'on'`
- Record video for each test.
`'retain-on-failure'`
- Record video for each test, but remove all videos from successful test runs.
`'on-first-retry'`
- Record video only when retrying a test for the first time.

Video files will appear in the test output directory, typically
`test-results`
. See
testOptions.video (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testoptions#test-options-video)
for advanced video configuration.

Videos are saved upon
browser context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts)
closure at the end of a test. If you create a browser context manually, make sure to await
browserContext.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-close)
.

Test
Library
playwright.config.ts
```
`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({use:{video:'on-first-retry',},});`
```
```
`constcontext=awaitbrowser.newContext({recordVideo:{dir:'videos/'}});// Make sure to await close, so that videos are saved.awaitcontext.close();`
```

You can also specify video size and annotation. The video size defaults to the viewport size scaled down to fit 800x800. The video of the viewport is placed in the top-left corner of the output video, scaled down to fit if necessary. You may need to set the viewport size to match your desired video size.

When
`show: { actions }`
is specified, each action will be visually highlighted in the video with the element outline and action title subtitle. The optional
`duration`
property controls how long each annotation is displayed (defaults to
`500`
ms).

When
`show: { test }`
is specified, video will be annotated with the current test information with configurable
`level`
.

playwright.config.ts
```
`import{defineConfig}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({use:{video:{mode:'on-first-retry',size:{width:640,height:480},show:{actions:{duration:500,position:'top-right',fontSize:14,},test:{level:'step',position:'top-left',fontSize:12,}},},},});`
```

For multi-page scenarios, you can access the video file associated with the page via the
page.video() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-video)
.

```
`constpath=awaitpage.video().path();`
```

note
Note that the video is only available after the page or browser context is closed.

user_input: I pulled a trace.zip off CI — how do I actually open it on my machine?
reference: Hand it to the CLI: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip.
reference_contexts: npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip
llm_response:
You can open your `trace.zip` file using one of the following methods:

*   **Playwright CLI:** Run the following command in your terminal, replacing `path/to/trace.zip` with the full path to your file:
    `npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`

*   **Browser:** Go to [trace.playwright.dev](https://trace.playwright.dev) and upload your file using drag and drop or the `Select file` button. This method loads the trace entirely in your browser without transmitting data externally.
llm_references: Trace viewer | Playwright

You can open a saved trace using either the Playwright CLI or in the browser at
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
. Make sure to add the full path to where your
`trace.zip`
file is located.

```
`npx playwright show-trace path/to/trace.zip`
```

trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
is a statically hosted variant of the Trace Viewer. You can upload a trace file using drag and drop or via the
`Select file`
button.

Trace Viewer loads the trace entirely in your browser and does not transmit any data externally.

You can open remote traces directly using its URL. This makes it easy to view the remote trace without having to manually download the file from CI runs, for example.

```
`npx playwright show-trace https://example.com/trace.zip`
```

When using
trace.playwright.dev (https://trace.playwright.dev)
, you can also pass the URL of your uploaded trace at some accessible storage (e.g. inside your CI) as a query parameter. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) rules might apply.

```
`https://trace.playwright.dev/?trace=https://demo.playwright.dev/reports/todomvc/data/e6099cadf79aa753d5500aa9508f9d1dbd87b5ee.zip`
```

user_input: How can I cap how many tests run in parallel straight from the command line?
reference: Bound the parallel worker count with the --workers flag, e.g. npx playwright test --workers 4.
reference_contexts: npx playwright test --workers 4
llm_response:
To cap the number of parallel tests from the command line, use the `--workers` flag. You can specify the number of workers as follows:

`npx playwright test --workers=4`

To disable parallelism entirely, set the value to 1:

`npx playwright test --workers=1`

command line (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-cli)
or in the
configuration file (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-configuration)
.

From the command line:

```
`npx playwrighttest--workers4`
```

In the configuration file:

playwright.config.ts
```

user_input: If my selector happens to match several elements and I try to click, what does Playwright do?
reference: It refuses to guess — locators are strict, so any action that needs one element throws when the locator resolves to more than one.
reference_contexts: Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:
llm_response:
If a locator matches more than one element, performing a click operation will throw an exception because locators are strict.

To resolve this, you should create a locator that uniquely identifies the target element. Alternatively, you can opt-out of the strictness check by using `locator.first()`, `locator.last()`, or `locator.nth()`, though these methods are not recommended because they may lead to clicking unintended elements if the page changes.
llm_references:
```
`awaitpage.getByRole('button').click();`
```

On the other hand, Playwright understands when you perform a multiple-element operation, so the following call works perfectly fine when the locator resolves to multiple elements.

Locators are strict. This means that all operations on locators that imply some target DOM element will throw an exception if more than one element matches. For example, the following call throws if there are several buttons in the DOM:

```
`awaitpage.getByRole('button').count();`
```

You can explicitly opt-out from strictness check by telling Playwright which element to use when multiple elements match, through
locator.first() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-first)
,
locator.last() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-last)
, and
locator.nth() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-nth)
. These methods are
not recommended
because when your page changes, Playwright may click on an element you did not intend. Instead, follow best practices above to create a locator that uniquely identifies the target element.

user_input: If my page throws up an alert or confirm and I never handle it, will my test get stuck?
reference: No — with no dialog listener registered, Playwright dismisses dialogs automatically, so they won't block the run.
reference_contexts: If there is no listener for page.on('dialog') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-dialog) , all dialogs are automatically dismissed.
llm_response:
No, your test will not get stuck if you do not handle the dialog. By default, Playwright automatically dismisses dialogs if there is no `page.on('dialog')` listener registered.

However, if you do register a `page.on('dialog')` listener, you must call either `dialog.accept()` or `dialog.dismiss()`. If you register a listener but fail to perform one of these actions, the page will freeze and your test actions will stall.

user_input: What's the pattern to trigger a file download and save it where I want?
reference: Arm the 'download' wait before the click (don't await it yet), click, await the download, then saveAs() using suggestedFilename().
llm_references: Downloads | Playwright

Added before v1.9

download.saveAs

Copy the download to a user-specified path. It is safe to call this method while the download is still in progress. Will wait for the download to finish if necessary.

Usage

```
`awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`
```

Arguments

`path`
string (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Data_structures#String_type)
# (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download#download-save-as-option-path)
Path where the download should be copied.

Returns

Promise (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Promise)
<
void (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/undefined)
>
# (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download#download-save-as-return)

Download | Playwright

Download (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download)
objects are dispatched by page via the
page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)
event.

All the downloaded files belonging to the browser context are deleted when the browser context is closed.

Download event is emitted once the download starts. Download path becomes available once download completes.

```
`// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`
```

For every attachment downloaded by the page,
page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)
event is emitted. All these attachments are downloaded into a temporary folder. You can obtain the download url, file name and payload stream using the
Download (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-download)
object from the event.

You can specify where to persist downloaded files using the
downloadsPath (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch-option-downloads-path)
option in
browserType.launch() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsertype#browser-type-launch)
.

note
Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.

Here is the simplest way to handle the file download:

```
`// Start waiting for download before clicking. Note no await.constdownloadPromise=page.waitForEvent('download');awaitpage.getByText('Download file').click();constdownload=awaitdownloadPromise;// Wait for the download process to complete and save the downloaded file somewhere.awaitdownload.saveAs('/path/to/save/at/'+download.suggestedFilename());`
```

`download`

user_input: Where should I keep saved login state, and how do I keep it out of version control?
reference: Stash it in a playwright/.auth directory and add that folder to .gitignore; tests then reuse the saved state to start already signed in.
reference_contexts: We recommend to create playwright/.auth directory and add it to your .gitignore . Your authentication routine will produce authenticated browser state and save it to a file in this playwright/.auth directory. Later on, tests will reuse this state and start already authenticated.
llm_response:
You should store authenticated browser state in a directory named `playwright/.auth` on the file system.

To keep this state out of version control, you must add the `playwright/.auth` directory to your `.gitignore` file. You can do this using the following commands:

*   **Bash:**
    ```bash
    mkdir -p playwright/.auth
    echo $'\nplaywright/.auth' >> .gitignore
    ```
*   **PowerShell:**
    ```powershell
    New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path playwright\.auth
    Add-Content -Path .gitignore "`r`nplaywright/.auth"
    ```
*   **Batch:**
    ```batch
    md playwright\.auth
    echo. >> .gitignore
    echo "playwright/.auth" >> .gitignore
    ```

Checking these files into repositories is strongly discouraged because they may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account.

`playwright/.auth`

Authentication | Playwright

This is the
recommended
approach for tests
without server-side state
. Authenticate once in the
setup project
, save the authentication state, and then reuse it to bootstrap each test already authenticated.

When to use

When you can imagine all your tests running at the same time with the same account, without affecting each other.

When not to use

Your tests modify server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting, and you run tests in parallel. In this case, tests must use different accounts.
Your authentication is browser-specific.

Details

Create
`tests/auth.setup.ts`
that will prepare authenticated browser state for all other tests.

tests/auth.setup.ts
```
`import{testassetup,expect}from'@playwright/test';importpathfrom'path';constauthFile=path.join(__dirname,'../playwright/.auth/user.json');setup('authenticate',async({page})=>{// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill('username');awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill('password');awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:authFile});});`
```

Create a new
`setup`
project in the config and declare it as a
dependency (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects#dependencies)
for all your testing projects. This project will always run and authenticate before all the tests. All testing projects should use the authenticated state as
`storageState`
.

playwright.config.ts
```
`import{defineConfig,devices}from'@playwright/test';exportdefaultdefineConfig({projects:[// Setup project{name:'setup',testMatch:/.*\.setup\.ts/},{name:'chromium',use:{...devices['Desktop Chrome'],// Use prepared auth state.storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json',},dependencies:['setup'],},{name:'firefox',use:{...devices['Desktop Firefox'],// Use prepared auth state.storageState:'playwright/.auth/user.json',},dependencies:['setup'],},],});`
```

Tests start already authenticated because we specified
`storageState`
in the config.

tests/example.spec.ts
```
`import{test}from'@playwright/test';test('test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated});`
```

Note that you need to delete the stored state when it expires. If you don't need to keep the state between test runs, write the browser state under
testProject.outputDir (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-output-dir)
, which is automatically cleaned up before every test run.

user_input: How do I interact with a button that's rendered inside an iframe?
reference: Step into the frame with frameLocator and then locate as usual — the getBy* methods exist on FrameLocator, so you can chain: page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click().

To interact with a button inside an iframe, you must first use a `FrameLocator` to target the iframe's content, and then use a locator method to find and interact with the button.

user_input: How do I split my tests to run across several machines at once?
reference: Shard with --shard=x/y — run 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4 on four machines so each takes a quarter of the suite.
reference_contexts:
npx playwright test --shard=1/4
npx playwright test --shard=2/4
npx playwright test --shard=3/4
npx playwright test --shard=4/4
llm_response:
To split your tests across several machines, you use the `--shard=x/y` command-line argument, where `x` is the current shard index and `y` is the total number of shards.

### Implementation
1. **Command:** Run your tests using `npx playwright test --shard=x/y` on each machine. For example, to split your suite into four shards, you would run:
   * `npx playwright test --shard=1/4`
   * `npx playwright test --shard=2/4`
   * `npx playwright test --shard=3/4`
   * `npx playwright test --shard=4/4`

2. **Balancing:** To ensure an even distribution of tests across shards, it is recommended to set `fullyParallel: true` in your `playwright.config.ts`. This enables test-level granularity. Without this setting, Playwright defaults to file-level granularity, which may lead to imbalanced shards if your test files vary significantly in size.

3. **Merging Reports:** Because each shard generates its own report, you should use the `blob` reporter to combine them:
   * Update your `playwright.config.ts` to use the blob reporter when running on CI:
     ```typescript
     reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',
     ```
   * After all shards complete, collect the generated blob reports into a single directory (e.g., `all-blob-reports`).
   * Run the merge command to produce a combined report:
     ```bash
     npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
     ```

### CI Integration
In a CI environment like GitHub Actions, you can automate this using a matrix strategy:
* Define a `matrix` with `shardTotal` (the total number of machines) and `shardIndex` (the specific index for each job).
* Use the `${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}` syntax in your test command.
* Upload the `blob-report` directory as an artifact from each job.
* Create a final job that depends on the test jobs (`needs: [playwright-tests]`), downloads all artifacts, and runs the `npx playwright merge-reports` command.
llm_references: Sharding | Playwright

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:

```
`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`
```

Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

GitHub Actions supports
sharding tests between multiple jobs (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-a-matrix-for-your-jobs)
using the
jobs.<job_id>.strategy.matrix (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/workflow-syntax-for-github-actions#jobsjob_idstrategymatrix)
option. The
`matrix`
option will run a separate job for every possible combination of the provided options.

The following example shows you how to configure a job to run your tests on four machines in parallel and then merge the reports into a single report. Don't forget to add
`reporter: process.env.CI ? 'blob' : 'html',`
to your
`playwright.config.ts`
file as in the example above.

First we add a
`matrix`
option to our job configuration with the
`shardTotal: [4]`
option containing the total number of shards we want to create and
`shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]`
with an array of the shard numbers.
Then we run our Playwright tests with the
`--shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }}`
option. This will run our test command for each shard.
Finally we upload our blob report to the GitHub Actions Artifacts. This will make the blob report available to other jobs in the workflow.

.github/workflows/playwright.yml
```
`name:Playwright Testson:push:branches:[main,master]pull_request:branches:[main,master]jobs:playwright-tests:timeout-minutes:60runs-on:ubuntu-lateststrategy:fail-fast:falsematrix:shardIndex:[1,2,3,4]shardTotal:[4]steps:-uses:actions/checkout@v5-uses:actions/setup-node@v5with:node-version:lts/*-name:Install dependenciesrun:npm ci-name:Install Playwright browsersrun:npx playwright install--with-deps-name:Run Playwright testsrun:npx playwright test--shard=${{matrix.shardIndex}}/${{matrix.shardTotal}}-name:Upload blob report to GitHub Actions Artifactsif:${{!cancelled()}}uses:actions/upload-artifact@v4with:name:blob-report-${{matrix.shardIndex}}path:blob-reportretention-days:1`
```

After all shards have completed, you can run a separate job that will merge the reports and produce a combined
HTML report (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#html-reporter)
. To ensure the execution order, we make the
`merge-reports`
job
depend (https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-jobs/using-jobs-in-a-workflow#defining-prerequisite-jobs)
on our sharded
`playwright-tests`
job by adding
`needs: [playwright-tests]`
.

.github/workflows/playwright.yml
```
`jobs:...merge-reports:# Merge reports after playwright-tests, even if some shards have failedif:${{!cancelled()}}needs:[playwright-tests]runs-on:ubuntu-lateststeps:-uses:actions/checkout@v5-uses:actions/setup-node@v5with:node-version:lts/*-name:Install dependenciesrun:npm ci-name:Download blob reports from GitHub Actions Artifactsuses:actions/download-artifact@v5with:path:all-blob-reportspattern:blob-report-*merge-multiple:true-name:Merge into HTML Reportrun:npx playwright merge-reports--reporter html ./all-blob-reports-name:Upload HTML reportuses:actions/upload-artifact@v4with:name:html-report--attempt-${{github.run_attempt}}path:playwright-reportretention-days:14`
```

You can now see the reports have been merged and a combined HTML report is available in the GitHub Actions Artifacts tab.

In the previous example, each test shard has its own test report. If you want to have a combined report showing all the test results from all the shards, you can merge them.

Start with adding
`blob`
reporter to the config when running on CI:

playwright.config.ts
```
`exportdefaultdefineConfig({testDir:'./tests',reporter:process.env.CI?'blob':'html',});`
```

Blob report contains information about all the tests that were run and their results as well as all test attachments such as traces and screenshot diffs. Blob reports can be merged and converted to any other Playwright report. By default, blob report will be generated into
`blob-report`
directory. You can learn about
blob report options here (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-reporters#blob-reporter)
.

To merge reports from multiple shards, put the blob report files into a single directory, for example
`all-blob-reports`
. Blob report names contain shard number, so they will not clash.

Afterwards, run
`npx playwright merge-reports`
command:

```
`npx playwright merge-reports--reporterhtml ./all-blob-reports`
```

This will produce a standard HTML report into
`playwright-report`
directory.

Sharding can be done at two levels of granularity depending on whether you use the
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
option or not. This affects how the tests are balanced across the shards.

Sharding with fullyParallel

When
`fullyParallel: true`
is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs. This is the preferred mode for ensuring even load distribution when sharding, as Playwright can optimize shard execution based on the total number of tests.

Sharding without fullyParallel

Without the fullyParallel setting, Playwright Test defaults to file-level granularity, meaning entire test files are assigned to shards (note that the same file may be assigned to different shards across different projects). In this case, the number of tests per file can greatly influence shard distribution. If your test files are not evenly sized (i.e., some files contain many more tests than others), certain shards may end up running significantly more tests, while others may run fewer or even none.

Key Takeaways:

With
`fullyParallel: true`
: Tests are split at the individual test level, leading to more balanced shard execution.
Without
`fullyParallel`
: Tests are split at the file level, so to balance the shards, it's important to keep your test files small and evenly sized.
To ensure the most effective use of sharding, especially in CI environments, it is recommended to use
`fullyParallel: true`
when aiming for balanced distribution across shards. Otherwise, you may need to manually organize your test files to avoid imbalances.

user_input: One test is genuinely slow and keeps timing out — is there a one-liner to give just it more room?
reference: Call test.slow() inside it; that marks the test slow and triples its timeout.
reference_contexts: test.slow() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-slow) marks the test as slow and triples the test timeout.
llm_response:
Yes, you can use one of the following one-liners inside your test function to increase the timeout:

*   **To triple the default timeout:** Use `test.slow();`.
*   **To set a specific timeout:** Use `test.setTimeout(120_000);` (where `120_000` is the timeout in milliseconds).
llm_references:
example.spec.ts
```
`import{test,expect}from'@playwright/test';test('slow test',async({page})=>{test.slow();// Easy way to triple the default timeout// ...});test('very slow test',async({page})=>{test.setTimeout(120_000);// ...});`
```

API reference:
test.setTimeout() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-set-timeout)
and
test.slow() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-test#test-slow)
.

Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and
`beforeEach`
hooks is included in the test timeout.

Timed out test produces the following error:

```
`example.spec.ts:3:1 › basic test ===========================Timeout of 30000ms exceeded.`
```

Additional separate timeout, of the same value, is shared between fixture teardowns and
`afterEach`
hooks, after the test function has finished.

The same timeout value also applies to
`beforeAll`
and
`afterAll`
hooks, but they do not share time with any test.

user_input: Why do teams add data-testid attributes instead of leaning on text or role?
reference: Test ids survive copy and role changes, so those tests keep passing even when the UI wording shifts — the downside is they aren't user-facing.
reference_contexts: Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass. QA's and developers should define explicit test ids and query them with page.getByTestId() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-test-id) . However testing by test ids is not user facing.
llm_response:
Teams add `data-testid` attributes because testing by test IDs is the most resilient way of testing; the test will still pass even if the text or role of the element changes.

Additionally, teams use test IDs when they choose to follow the test ID methodology or when they are unable to locate an element by role or text.
llm_references:
Testing by test ids is the most resilient way of testing as even if your text or role of the attribute changes, the test will still pass. QA's and developers should define explicit test ids and query them with
page.getByTestId() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-test-id)
. However testing by test ids is not user facing. If the role or text value is important to you then consider using user facing locators such as
role (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-role)
and
text locators (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-text)
.

For example, consider the following DOM structure.

http://localhost:3000
Itinéraire
```
`<buttondata-testid="directions">Itinéraire</button>`
```

You can locate the element by its test id:

```
`awaitpage.getByTestId('directions').click();`
```

When to use testid locators
You can also use test ids when you choose to use the test id methodology or when you can't locate by
role (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-role)
or
text (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-text)
.

Playwright comes with multiple built-in locators. To make tests resilient, we recommend prioritizing user-facing attributes and explicit contracts such as
page.getByRole() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-role)
.

For example, consider the following DOM structure.

http://localhost:3000
Sign in
```
`<button>Sign in</button>`
```

Locate the element by its role of
`button`
with name "Sign in".

```
`awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();`
```

note
Use the
code generator (https://playwright.dev/docs/codegen)
to generate a locator, and then edit it as you'd like.

Every time a locator is used for an action, an up-to-date DOM element is located in the page. In the snippet below, the underlying DOM element will be located twice, once prior to every action. This means that if the DOM changes in between the calls due to re-render, the new element corresponding to the locator will be used.

```
`constlocator=page.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'});awaitlocator.hover();awaitlocator.click();`
```

Note that all methods that create a locator, such as
page.getByLabel() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-get-by-label)
, are also available on the
Locator (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator)
and
FrameLocator (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-framelocator)
classes, so you can chain them and iteratively narrow down your locator.

```
`constlocator=page.frameLocator('#my-frame').getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'});awaitlocator.click();`
```

warning
We recommend
locating by test id (https://playwright.dev/docs/locators#locate-by-test-id)
instead.

Playwright supports shorthand for selecting elements using certain attributes. Currently, only the following attributes are supported:

`id`
`data-testid`
`data-test-id`
`data-test`

```
`// Fill an input with the id "username"awaitpage.locator('id=username').fill('value');// Click an element with data-test-id "submit"awaitpage.locator('data-test-id=submit').click();`
```

note
Attribute selectors are not CSS selectors, so anything CSS-specific like
`:enabled`
is not supported. For more features, use a proper
css (https://playwright.dev/docs/other-locators#css-locator)
selector, e.g.
`css=[data-test="login"]:enabled`
.

user_input: My e2e tests mutate shared server state and run in parallel. What auth model avoids collisions, and how do workers stay on separate accounts?
reference: Give each parallel worker its own account and authenticate it once with a worker-scoped fixture. Key the account on the worker's parallelIndex — which stays the same even when a worker restarts — so a worker always maps to the same account.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach for tests that modify server-side state . In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

Each worker process is assigned two ids: a unique worker index that starts with 1, and a parallel index that is between 0 and workers - 1 . When a worker is restarted, for example after a failure, the new worker process has the same parallelIndex and a new workerIndex .
llm_response:
The recommended approach for tests that mutate shared server-side state is to use **one account per parallel worker**.

To implement this, you must create a `playwright/fixtures.ts` file that overrides the `storageState` fixture to authenticate once per worker. Workers stay on separate accounts by using `test.info().parallelIndex` as a unique identifier to differentiate between them.

### Implementation Steps:
1. **Create a worker-scoped fixture**: In `playwright/fixtures.ts`, define a `workerStorageState` fixture with `{scope: 'worker'}`.
2. **Differentiate workers**: Use `test.info().parallelIndex` to assign a unique account to each worker process. You can either create a new account dynamically or use a list of pre-created accounts.
3. **Override `storageState`**: Use the `workerStorageState` fixture to provide the authentication state to all tests running within that specific worker.
4. **Update tests**: Import `test` from your custom `playwright/fixtures.ts` file in your test files instead of `@playwright/test`.

You can perform the authentication steps either via the UI (as shown in excerpt [2]) or via an API request using `request.newContext` (as shown in excerpt [3]).

This is the
recommended
approach for tests that
modify server-side state
. In Playwright, worker processes run in parallel. In this approach, each parallel worker is authenticated once. All tests ran by worker are reusing the same authentication state. We will need multiple testing accounts, one per each parallel worker.

When to use

Your tests modify shared server-side state. For example, one test checks the rendering of the settings page, while the other test is changing the setting.

When not to use

Your tests do not modify any shared server-side state. In this case, all tests can use a single shared account.

Details

We will authenticate once per
worker process (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel#worker-processes)
, each with a unique account.

Create
`playwright/fixtures.ts`
file that will
override storageState fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#overriding-fixtures)
to authenticate once per worker. Use
testInfo.parallelIndex (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testinfo#test-info-parallel-index)
to differentiate between workers.

playwright/fixtures.ts
```
`import{testasbaseTest,expect}from'@playwright/test';importfsfrom'fs';importpathfrom'path';export*from'@playwright/test';exportconsttest=baseTest.extend<{},{workerStorageState:string}>({// Use the same storage state for all tests in this worker.storageState:({workerStorageState},use)=>use(workerStorageState),// Authenticate once per worker with a worker-scoped fixture.workerStorageState:[async({browser},use)=>{// Use parallelIndex as a unique identifier for each worker.constid=test.info().parallelIndex;constfileName=path.resolve(test.info().project.outputDir,`.auth/${id}.json`);if(fs.existsSync(fileName)){// Reuse existing authentication state if any.awaituse(fileName);return;}// Important: make sure we authenticate in a clean environment by unsetting storage state.constpage=awaitbrowser.newPage({storageState:undefined});// Acquire a unique account, for example create a new one.// Alternatively, you can have a list of precreated accounts for testing.// Make sure that accounts are unique, so that multiple team members// can run tests at the same time without interference.constaccount=awaitacquireAccount(id);// Perform authentication steps. Replace these actions with your own.awaitpage.goto('https://github.com/login');awaitpage.getByLabel('Username or email address').fill(account.username);awaitpage.getByLabel('Password').fill(account.password);awaitpage.getByRole('button',{name:'Sign in'}).click();// Wait until the page receives the cookies.//// Sometimes login flow sets cookies in the process of several redirects.// Wait for the final URL to ensure that the cookies are actually set.awaitpage.waitForURL('https://github.com/');// Alternatively, you can wait until the page reaches a state where all cookies are set.awaitexpect(page.getByRole('button',{name:'View profile and more'})).toBeVisible();// End of authentication steps.awaitpage.context().storageState({path:fileName});awaitpage.close();awaituse(fileName);},{scope:'worker'}],});`
```

Now, each test file should import
`test`
from our fixtures file instead of
`@playwright/test`
. No changes are needed in the config.

tests/example.spec.ts
```
`// Important: import our fixtures.import{test,expect}from'../playwright/fixtures';test('test',async({page})=>{// page is authenticated});`
```

When to use

Your web application supports authenticating via API that is easier/faster than interacting with the app UI.

Details

We will send the API request with
APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
and then save authenticated state as usual.

In the
setup project (https://playwright.dev/docs/auth#basic-shared-account-in-all-tests)
:

tests/auth.setup.ts
```
`import{testassetup}from'@playwright/test';constauthFile='playwright/.auth/user.json';setup('authenticate',async({request})=>{// Send authentication request. Replace with your own.awaitrequest.post('https://github.com/login',{form:{'user':'user','password':'password'}});awaitrequest.storageState({path:authFile});});`

user_input: Two problems with how our team writes tests. The recorder is the fastest way for people to get started, but the selectors it emits break on the next refactor, and half our app is behind a login so recording anything past the sign-in page means clicking through the form by hand every single time. Are both of these things the recorder can be told to handle?
reference: Both are, and they're separate mechanisms. On selectors: the generator isn't emitting raw CSS by accident — it inspects the page and picks what it judges the best locator, prioritising role, text and test id locators in that order, and when a candidate matches several elements it refines it until it uniquely identifies the target. So brittle output is usually a signal about the markup rather than the tool: give the elements you care about a test id (or accessible roles and names) and the recorder will prefer those. You can also use Pick Locator to grab and hand-tune a single locator rather than recording a whole flow. On the login: record the authentication once with `npx playwright codegen <url> --save-storage=auth.json`, which writes the cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB state at the end of the session, then start every later recording with `npx playwright codegen --load-storage=auth.json <url>`, which restores that state so the app comes up already signed in and you record only the part you care about. That saved state is the same kind of artifact your suite consumes as storageState, so the recorded flow and the running tests can share it.
reference_contexts: Playwright will look at your page and figure out the best locator, prioritizing role, text and test id locators. If the generator finds multiple elements matching the locator, it will improve the locator to make it resilient that uniquely identifies the target element.

Run codegen with --save-storage to save cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data at the end of the session. This is useful to separately record an authentication step and reuse it later when recording more tests.

Run with --load-storage to consume the previously loaded storage from the auth.json. This way, all cookies, localStorage and IndexedDB data will be restored, bringing most web apps to the authenticated state without the need to login again. This means you can continue generating tests from the logged in state.
You can generate locators with the test generator.

Yes, the recorder can be told to handle both of these issues:

*   **Resilient Selectors:** The test generator is designed to prioritize role, text, and test id locators. If it finds multiple elements matching a locator, it automatically improves the locator to make it resilient and uniquely identify the target element.
*   **Authentication:** You can avoid manual logins by preserving and loading the authenticated state. 
    *   First, record the authentication step once and save the state by running `npx playwright codegen --save-storage=auth.json`.

user_input: When I shard across CI jobs, how do workers, fullyParallel and retries interact to keep runs balanced and reliable?
reference: Inside each shard Playwright still runs worker processes; turning on fullyParallel shards at the individual-test level so each job gets an even slice rather than whole files. Keep retries enabled so that when a worker is torn down after a failure it simply restarts and re-runs the affected test.
reference_contexts: When fullyParallel: true is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs.
Workers are always shutdown after a test failure (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-retries#failures) to guarantee pristine environment for following tests.
If you enable retries , second worker process will start by retrying the failed test and continue from there.
llm_response:
To keep runs balanced and reliable when sharding across CI jobs, the interaction between workers, `fullyParallel`, and retries functions as follows:

### Balancing Shards
*   **`fullyParallel`**: This is the recommended setting for balanced distribution. When `fullyParallel: true` is enabled, Playwright splits tests at the individual test level, allowing it to distribute tests evenly across shards. Without this setting, Playwright defaults to file-level granularity, which can lead to imbalances if test files are not evenly sized.
*   **Workers**: You can control the number of parallel worker processes to optimize the utilization of CPU cores on the machines running your shards. While sharding splits the test suite into parts across different machines, workers determine how many tests run in parallel within each individual shard/machine.

### Reliability
*   **Retries**: Playwright supports retries to handle flaky tests. When enabled (via the command line `--retries` or in the configuration file), failing tests are re-run until they pass or the maximum number of retries is reached. 
*   **Interaction with Sharding**: Retries are handled within the shard where the test was originally assigned. You can detect if a test is being retried at runtime using `testInfo.retry`, which allows you to perform specific actions (like cleaning server-side state) to ensure the retry is reliable.
*   **CI Integration**: When using sharding in CI, it is recommended to use the `blob` reporter for individual shards and then merge the reports into a single HTML report after all shards have completed. This ensures that even if some shards have failures or retries, the final combined report provides a complete view of the test suite.

To

Sharding can be done at two levels of granularity depending on whether you use the
testProject.fullyParallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-testproject#test-project-fully-parallel)
option or not. This affects how the tests are balanced across the shards.

Sharding with fullyParallel

When
`fullyParallel: true`
is enabled, Playwright Test runs individual tests in parallel across multiple shards, ensuring each shard receives an even distribution of tests. This allows for test-level granularity, meaning each shard will attempt to balance the number of individual tests it runs. This is the preferred mode for ensuring even load distribution when sharding, as Playwright can optimize shard execution based on the total number of tests.

Sharding without fullyParallel

Without the fullyParallel setting, Playwright Test defaults to file-level granularity, meaning entire test files are assigned to shards (note that the same file may be assigned to different shards across different projects). In this case, the number of tests per file can greatly influence shard distribution. If your test files are not evenly sized (i.e., some files contain many more tests than others), certain shards may end up running significantly more tests, while others may run fewer or even none.

Key Takeaways:

With
`fullyParallel: true`
: Tests are split at the individual test level, leading to more balanced shard execution.
Without
`fullyParallel`
: Tests are split at the file level, so to balance the shards, it's important to keep your test files small and evenly sized.
To ensure the most effective use of sharding, especially in CI environments, it is recommended to use
`fullyParallel: true`
when aiming for balanced distribution across shards. Otherwise, you may need to manually organize your test files to avoid imbalances.

By default, Playwright runs test files in
parallel (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
and strives for optimal utilization of CPU cores on your machine. In order to achieve even greater parallelisation, you can further scale Playwright test execution by running tests on multiple machines simultaneously. We call this mode of operation "sharding". Sharding in Playwright means splitting your tests into smaller parts called "shards". Each shard is like a separate job that can run independently. The whole purpose is to divide your tests to speed up test runtime.

When you shard your tests, each shard can run on its own, utilizing the available CPU cores. This helps speed up the testing process by doing tasks simultaneously.

In a CI pipeline, each shard can run as a separate job, making use of the hardware resources available in your CI pipeline, like CPU cores, to run tests faster.

To shard the test suite, pass
`--shard=x/y`
to the command line. For example, to split the suite into four shards, each running one fourth of the tests:

```
`npx playwrighttest--shard=1/4npx playwrighttest--shard=2/4npx playwrighttest--shard=3/4npx playwrighttest--shard=4/4`
```

Now, if you run these shards in parallel on different jobs, your test suite completes four times faster.

Note that Playwright can only shard tests that can be run in parallel. By default, this means Playwright will shard test files. Learn about other options in the
parallelism guide (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-parallel)
.

user_input: Should I use a globalSetup file or project dependencies for one-time setup, and why?
reference: Prefer project dependencies. Because a dependency is a real project that runs ahead of the others, it plugs into the runner properly — the setup shows up in the HTML report, is traced, and can use fixtures — whereas globalSetup misses some of that.
reference_contexts: This is the recommended approach, as it integrates better with the Playwright test runner: your HTML report will include the global setup, traces will be recorded, and fixtures can be used.

Dependencies are a list of projects that need to run before the tests in another project run. They can be useful for configuring the global setup actions so that one project depends on this running first.
llm_response:
You should use project dependencies. It is the recommended approach because it integrates better with the Playwright test runner.

Compared to the `globalSetup` config option, project dependencies provide the following advantages:
* **HTML report visibility:** Global setup is shown as a separate project in the report.
* **Trace recording:** Full trace recording is available.
* **Playwright fixtures:** Fully supported.
* **Browser management:** Handled via the `browser` fixture rather than manual `browserType.launch()` calls.
* **Parallelism and retries:** Supported via standard configuration.
* **Config options:** Settings like `headless` or `testIdAttribute` are automatically applied.

In contrast, the `globalSetup` config option does not support traces or fixtures, is not shown in the HTML report, ignores standard config options, and requires manual browser management. The documentation explicitly advises considering project dependencies instead of `globalSetup` to ensure full feature support.

user_input: Our app registers a service worker for offline support. Every route handler I install works fine against a build with the worker disabled, but against the real build some requests reach the network untouched while others are intercepted, and which is which seems to change between runs. What decides whether a request is interceptable here, and what's the sane way to test against this app?
reference: Whether a request is routable depends on who owns it. Once a service worker with a fetch handler is installed it sits between the page and the network: the page-owned request is served by the worker and never reaches the network, so it isn't routable, while the worker's own outbound request is a separate, service-worker-owned request that context routing does see. That split is why interception looks inconsistent — you're catching some requests at one layer and missing others at the other, and which layer serves a given resource depends on the worker's cache state, hence the run-to-run variation. If you're doing ordinary network mocking, the documented answer is not to reason about this at all: set `serviceWorkers: 'block'` in the config's `use` options so the worker never registers and everything is page-owned and routable. Only if you specifically need to assert on the worker's own traffic should you leave them enabled and branch inside the handler on `route.request().serviceWorker()` — noting that calling .frame() on such a request throws, and that requests for updated worker scripts cannot currently be routed at all.
reference_contexts: If you're looking to do general network mocking, routing, and interception, please see the Network Guide first. Playwright provides built-in APIs for this use case that don't require the information below. However, if you're interested in requests made by Service Workers themselves, please read below.
To disable service workers, set testOptions.serviceWorkers to 'block'.

llm_response:
Whether a request is interceptable depends on whether it is owned by the Frame or the Service Worker. When a Service Worker has a `fetch` handler registered, requests made by the page are handled by the Service Worker. In this scenario, the Frame-owned request events are not routable because they do not hit the external network; instead, the Service Worker-owned request is the one that can be routed via `browserContext.route()`.

The sane way to test against this app depends on your goals:

*   **To make tests more predictable and performant:** Disable Service Workers entirely by setting `testOptions.serviceWorkers` to `'block'` in your `playwright.config.ts`.
*   **To perform general network mocking and routing:** Use Playwright's built-in Network APIs (as described in the Network Guide) rather than relying on Service Worker interception.
*   **If you must test the Service Worker's behavior:** You can use `browserContext.route()` to intercept requests made by the Service Worker itself. You can identify these requests because `request.serviceWorker()` will be set to the Service Worker instance, and calling `request.frame()` on them will throw an exception. Additionally, you can verify if a response was handled by a Service Worker's fetch handler by checking if `response.fromServiceWorker()` returns `true`.

user_input: Our GitHub Actions job installs cleanly — `npm ci` is green — and then every test fails at browser launch complaining about missing shared libraries. It's an ubuntu-latest runner, and the identical commit runs fine on all three of our developers' machines. What is the CI box missing that a laptop already has, and what's the durable way to fix it?
reference: Installing the npm package is not the same as provisioning a machine that can run browsers, and that's the gap. `npm ci` fetches the library; the browser binaries are downloaded separately, and those binaries need operating-system level libraries that a developer machine already has from everyday browser use and a bare Linux runner does not. So there are two things to install, and the combined step is `npx playwright install --with-deps`, which fetches the browsers and the OS dependencies together — that's exactly the step the recommended GitHub Actions workflow runs between `npm ci` and the test command. The alternative, and the more durable one if you also do visual comparison, is to run the job inside the official container image via `jobs.<job_id>.container`: it keeps the dependencies out of the host environment and gives you a consistent rendering environment, which matters because screenshots differ across platforms.
reference_contexts: Ensure CI agent can run browsers: Use our Docker image in Linux agents or install your dependencies using the CLI.
# Install NPM packages npm ci # Install Playwright browsers and dependencies npx playwright install --with-deps
The Command line tools can be used to install all operating system dependencies in CI.

GitHub Actions support running jobs in a container by using the jobs.<job_id>.container option. This is useful to not pollute the host environment with dependencies and to have a consistent environment for e.g. screenshots/visual regression testing across different operating systems.
llm_response:
The CI environment is missing the necessary system dependencies required to run browsers, which are present on local machines but not pre-installed on standard `ubuntu-latest` runners.

To fix this durably, you should use the Playwright CLI to install both the browsers and the required OS dependencies in your CI configuration. The recommended approach is to run the following command after installing your NPM packages:

```bash
npx playwright install --with-deps
```

Alternatively, if you only need to install the system dependencies without re-installing the browsers, you can use:

```bash
npx playwright install-deps
```

You can also target a specific browser (e.g., `chromium`) by passing it as an argument to either command.
llm_references:
System dependencies can get installed automatically. This is useful for CI environments.

```
`npx playwright install-deps`
```

You can also install the dependencies for a single browser by passing it as an argument:

```
`npx playwright install-deps chromium`
```

It's also possible to combine
`install-deps`
with
`install`
so that the browsers and OS dependencies are installed with a single command.

```
`npx playwrightinstall--with-deps chromium`
```

See
system requirements (https://playwright.dev/docs/intro#system-requirements)
for officially supported operating systems.

user_input: Almost all of our tests stub the search endpoint so they're hermetic, and that's been great until the backend quietly renamed a field and every test stayed green while production broke. I want to keep most tests stubbed but have a couple that exercise the real endpoint and only override one flag in whatever comes back. Can the same interception mechanism do both, and what changes between them?
reference: Both go through the same route handler; what differs is whether you ever let the request reach the network. A hermetic stub never does: page.route(url, route => route.fulfill({ json: ... })) answers from the test and the server is never contacted, which is why a server-side shape change can't fail it. To modify a real response you have to fetch it first — inside the handler call `const response = await route.fetch()`, read the real body with `await response.json()`, mutate the field you care about, and then fulfill with the edited payload: `await route.fulfill({ response, json })`. That gives you the real contract for everything you didn't touch, so the renamed field would have surfaced. Routes are matched most-recently-registered first and are scoped to the page or context they were registered on, so a spec-level `page.route` override can sit on top of a project-wide stub. If you want the real traffic recorded once and replayed thereafter, that's what HAR replay is for.
reference_contexts: Mock API requests: All the requests made by the page, including XHRs and fetch requests, can be tracked, modified and mocked.
await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => { const json = [{ name: 'Strawberry', id: 21 }]; await route.fulfill({ json }); });

await page.route('*/**/api/v1/fruits', async route => { const response = await route.fetch(); const json = await response.json(); json.push({ name: 'Loquat', id: 100 }); // Fulfill using the original response, while patching the response body with the given JSON object. await route.fulfill({ response, json }); });

To modify a response use
APIRequestContext (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-apirequestcontext)
to get the original response and then pass the response to
route.fulfill() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-route#route-fulfill)
. You can override individual fields on the response via options:

```
`awaitpage.route('**/title.html',asyncroute=>{// Fetch original response.constresponse=awaitroute.fetch();// Add a prefix to the title.letbody=awaitresponse.text();body=body.replace('<title>','<title>My prefix:');awaitroute.fulfill({// Pass all fields from the response.response,// Override response body.body,// Force content type to be html.headers:{...response.headers(),'content-type':'text/html'}});});`
```

Sometimes, it is essential to make an API request, but the response needs to be patched to allow for reproducible testing. In that case, instead of mocking the request, one can perform the request and fulfill it with the modified response.

user_input: How does device emulation (viewport, user agent, touch) get applied per test, and why doesn't it bleed into other tests?
reference: Device parameters come from Playwright's device registry and are applied at the browser-context level. Since every test runs in its own isolated context — which can also carry mobile emulation, permissions, locale and color scheme — the emulation stays scoped to that test.
reference_contexts: Playwright comes with a registry of device parameters (https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/blob/main/packages/playwright-core/src/server/deviceDescriptorsSource.json) using playwright.devices (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-playwright#playwright-devices) for selected desktop, tablet and mobile devices. It can be used to simulate browser behavior for a specific device such as user agent, screen size, viewport and if it has touch enabled. All tests will run with the specified device parameters.

Browser contexts can also be used to emulate multi-page scenarios involving mobile devices, permissions, locale and color scheme. Check out our Emulation (https://playwright.dev/docs/emulation) guide for more details.
llm_response:
Device emulation is applied by configuring browser contexts with specific parameters, such as those found in the `playwright.devices` registry (which includes viewport, user agent, and touch/`isMobile` settings).

### How it is applied
You can apply these settings at different levels:
*   **Global/Project level:** In `playwright.config.ts`, you can define projects that use specific device descriptors or custom settings within the `use` object.
*   **Test/Suite level:** You can use `test.use()` within a test file or `test.describe()` block to apply specific emulation settings (like `viewport` or `userAgent`) to those tests.
*   **Manual context creation:** When using the library directly, you pass the emulation parameters into `browser.newContext({...})`.
*   **Page level:** For viewports specifically, you can override the context setting for an individual page using `page.setViewportSize()`.

### Why it doesn't bleed into other tests
Emulation settings do not bleed between tests because Playwright achieves test isolation using **Browser Contexts**. 
*   Each test is assigned its own unique `BrowserContext`, which acts as an incognito-like profile.
*   When using the Playwright Test Runner, a new browser context is created automatically for every test.
*   Because every test runs in its own isolated context, any emulation parameters applied to one context (via `test.use` or `browser.newContext`) are contained strictly within that context and do not affect the browser state, storage, or emulation settings of other tests.

user_input: One fixture is slow, but I don't want to inflate every test's timeout. How do fixture and test timeouts relate, and what's the fix?
reference: A fixture's setup counts against the test's clock, so a sluggish one can trip test timeouts. Hand that fixture its own longer timeout through the tuple option and leave the test's timeout tight.
reference_contexts: By default, fixture (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures) shares timeout with the test. However, for slow fixtures, especially worker-scoped (https://playwright.dev/docs/test-fixtures#worker-scoped-fixtures) ones, it is convenient to have a separate timeout. This way you can keep the overall test timeout small, and give the slow fixture more time.

Fixture is considered to be a part of a test, and so its setup and teardown running time counts towards the test timeout. Therefore, a slow fixture may cause test timeouts. You can set a separate larger timeout for such a fixture, and keep the overall test timeout small.

```

user_input: Our CI machines are a lot slower than our laptops and I've been sprinkling per-assertion timeouts around to get the suite green, which is clearly the wrong shape. Some tests now fail with a message about the test itself rather than the assertion, and raising the assertion timeout further doesn't help those at all. How many separate budgets am I actually dealing with, and which one do I raise?
reference: Three budgets, nested, which is why raising the wrong one does nothing. The test timeout is 30 seconds by default and covers the whole test — the test function plus fixture setup plus beforeEach hooks — and it's what you're hitting when the failure names the test rather than an assertion; raise it in the config's `timeout`, or per test with test.setTimeout(120_000), or test.slow() to triple the default. Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have their own separate 5-second expect timeout, which is unrelated to the test timeout and is the one reported in a 'expect.toHaveText with timeout 5000ms' call log; set it globally with `expect: { timeout: 10_000 }` or per assertion with a { timeout } option. Because the assertion budget is consumed inside the test budget, pushing the expect timeout above the test timeout accomplishes nothing — the test dies first. beforeAll/afterAll get their own timeout, equal to the test timeout by default and adjustable inside the hook. The right fix for a uniformly slower machine is the config-level defaults, not per-assertion overrides.
reference_contexts: Playwright Test enforces a timeout for each test, 30 seconds by default. Time spent by the test function, fixture setups, and beforeEach hooks is included in the test timeout.
Auto-retrying assertions like expect(locator).toHaveText() have a separate timeout, 5 seconds by default. Assertion timeout is unrelated to the test timeout.
export default defineConfig({ expect: { timeout: 10_000, }, });
test('very slow test', async ({ page }) => { test.setTimeout(120_000); }); test.slow(); // Easy way to triple the default timeout
beforeAll and afterAll hooks have a separate timeout, by default equal to test timeout. You can change it separately for each hook by calling testInfo.setTimeout() inside the hook.
llm_response:
You are dealing with two separate timeout budgets:

1.  **Test timeout:** This covers the test function, fixture setups, `beforeEach` hooks, and (separately) fixture teardowns and `afterEach` hooks. It also applies to `beforeAll` and `afterAll` hooks. The default is 30,000 ms.
2.  **Expect timeout:** This covers each individual assertion. The default is 5,000 ms.

Since you mentioned that raising the assertion timeout does not help with failures that report on the test itself, you are hitting the **Test timeout**. You should raise the test timeout instead of the expect timeout.

You can increase the test timeout in the following ways:
*   **In the config:** Set `{ timeout: 60_000 }` (or your desired value).
*   **In the test:** Use `test.setTimeout(120_000)`.

user_input: What's the reliable way to select a parent row based on a child element, and why avoid xpath=.. for it?
reference: Filter the parent by the child locator — e.g. getByRole('listitem').filter({ has: child }) — which is evaluated relative to the parent match. xpath=.. works but is brittle: any DOM change can break it, so prefer filtering.
reference_contexts: The filtering locator must be relative to the original locator and is queried starting with the original locator match, not the document root.

Alternatively, if you cannot find a suitable locator for the parent element, use xpath=.. . Note that this method is not as reliable, because any changes to the DOM structure will break your tests. Prefer locator.filter() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-filter) when possible.

user_input: Before a click, what does Playwright verify, and how does that relate to the waiting a plain click already does?
reference: A click runs actionability checks — attached, visible, stable, receives pointer events, enabled — and auto-waits for them. The pointer methods bake that same sequence in (down to scrolling into view), so you rarely need explicit waits.
reference_contexts: Playwright performs a range of actionability checks on the elements before making actions to ensure these actions behave as expected. It auto-waits for all the relevant checks to pass and only then performs the requested action. If the required checks do not pass within the given timeout , action fails with the TimeoutError .
wait for element with given selector to be in DOM
llm_response:
Before performing a click, Playwright verifies the following:

*   **Locator resolution:** The locator must resolve to exactly one element.
*   **Visibility:** The element must be visible (not empty, no `display:none`, and no `visibility:hidden`).
*   **Stability:** The element must be stable, meaning it is not animating or has completed its animation.
*   **Receiving Events:** The element must be able to receive pointer events at the action point (it must not be obscured by other elements).
*   **Enabled state:** The element must be enabled.

These checks are part of Playwright's "auto-waiting" mechanism. Playwright automatically waits for all these relevant checks to pass before performing the click. If these checks do not pass within the specified `timeout`, the action fails with a `TimeoutError`.

This relates to the waiting a plain click performs by ensuring the element is ready for interaction. Specifically, the process includes:
1.  Waiting for the element to be in the DOM.
2.  Waiting for it to become displayed.
3.  Waiting for it to stop moving (e.g., until CSS transitions finish).
4.  Scrolling the element into view.
5.  Waiting for it to receive pointer events at the action point.
6.  Retrying if the element is detached during any of these checks.

`timeout`
, action fails with the
`TimeoutError`
.

For example, for
locator.click() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-locator#locator-click)
, Playwright will ensure that:

user_input: Where do downloaded files go, and why might they disappear before I can use them?
reference: Downloaded files sit in a temporary folder and belong to whichever context fetched them, so they vanish the instant that context is torn down. Each test gets a freshly created context, so grab anything you need before the test ends.
reference_contexts: Downloaded files are deleted when the browser context that produced them is closed.
Playwright uses browser contexts to achieve Test Isolation. Each test has its own Browser Context. Running the test creates a new browser context each time.
llm_response:
Downloaded files are stored in a temporary folder by default. You can specify a different location to persist files by using the `downloadsPath` option in `browserType.launch()`.

Files may disappear before you can use them because all downloaded files belonging to a browser context are deleted when that browser context is closed.

page.on('download') (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-page#page-event-download)

All the downloaded files belonging to the browser context are deleted when the browser context is closed.

user_input: My manually-created context never produced a video file. How is video capture tied to the context lifecycle?
reference: Video is flushed when the browser context closes. With the test runner that happens automatically, but if you created the context yourself you must await context.close(), or the file won't be written.
reference_contexts: Videos are saved upon browser context (https://playwright.dev/docs/browser-contexts) closure at the end of a test. If you create a browser context manually, make sure to await browserContext.close() (https://playwright.dev/docs/api/class-browsercontext#browser-context-close) .
When using Playwright as a Test Runner, browser contexts are created by default. Otherwise, you can create browser contexts manually.
llm_response:
Video capture is tied to the browser context lifecycle because videos are only saved upon the closure of the browser context. If you create a browser context manually, you must `await browserContext.close()` to ensure the video file is written to the filesystem. 

The video is guaranteed to be written to the filesystem once the browser context is closed. Consequently, the video file is only available after the page or browser context has been closed.
llm_references:

`'retain-on-failure'`

`'on-first-retry'`

Video files will appear in the test output directory, typically
